title: Chapter 6
paragraphs: Alexey Alexandrovitch had won a brilliant victory at the session of the Commission of August 17th, but in the aftermath that victory cut the ground out from under him. The new commission for the inquiry into the condition of the native tribes in every aspect had been formed and dispatched to its destination with an uncommon speed and energy that came from Alexey Alexandrovitch himself. Within three months a report was delivered. The condition of the native tribes had been examined in its political, administrative, economic, ethnographic, material, and religious aspects. To every one of these questions the report offered admirably stated answers, answers admitting no shade of doubt — for they were not the product of human thought, which is always liable to error, but the product of official activity. All of them rested on official data supplied by governors and heads of churches, founded on the reports of district magistrates and ecclesiastical superintendents, founded in turn on the reports of parochial overseers and parish priests; so every answer was unhesitating and certain. Questions such as why crops fail, why certain tribes cling to their ancient beliefs, and so on — questions which, without the convenient intervention of the official machinery, are not and cannot be settled for ages — received full, confident solutions. And those solutions all favored Alexey Alexandrovitch's contention. But Stremov, stung to the quick at the last session, had, on receipt of the commission's report, resorted to a tactic Alexey Alexandrovitch had not foreseen. Stremov, bringing several members along with him, crossed over to Alexey Alexandrovitch's side, and not content with warmly defending the measure Karenin had proposed, put forward other, more extreme measures in the same direction. These measures, exaggerated still further beyond Alexey Alexandrovitch's original idea, were passed by the commission — and then Stremov's strategy became clear. Pushed to the extreme, the measures suddenly looked so absurd that the highest authorities, public opinion, intellectual ladies, and the newspapers all at once turned on them, expressing their indignation both with the measures and with their nominal author, Alexey Alexandrovitch. Stremov drew back, pretending he had simply followed Karenin's lead and was now astonished and distressed at the result. That meant Alexey Alexandrovitch's defeat. But despite his failing health, despite his domestic troubles, he did not give in. The commission split. Some members, headed by Stremov, justified their mistake by saying they had put their trust in the revising commission Alexey Alexandrovitch had set up, and now declared the commission's report worthless — so much waste paper. Alexey Alexandrovitch, with a following of those who saw the danger of so revolutionary an attitude toward official documents, kept defending the statements obtained by the revising commission. As a result, in the upper spheres — and even in society at large — everything was in confusion, and although everyone was interested, no one could say whether the native tribes really were sinking into poverty and ruin or whether they were thriving. Alexey Alexandrovitch's position, partly because of this and partly because of the contempt heaped on him for his wife's infidelity, became very precarious. And in this position he took an important decision. To the astonishment of the commission, he announced that he would request permission to go and investigate the question himself, on the spot. Having obtained permission, Alexey Alexandrovitch prepared to set out for those distant provinces.
Alexey Alexandrovitch's departure made a great stir, all the more because just before leaving he officially returned the posting fares allotted to him for twelve horses to drive to his destination.
"I think it very noble," Betsy said about it to Princess Myakaya. "Why take money for posting horses when everyone knows there are railways everywhere now?"
But Princess Myakaya disagreed, and Princess Tverskaya's opinion in fact irritated her.

"It's all very well for you to talk," she said, "when you have I don't know how many millions; but I'm always glad when my husband goes off on a revising tour in the summer. It's good for him, pleasant traveling about, and we have a settled arrangement that I keep a carriage and coachman on the money."
On the way to the distant provinces, Alexey Alexandrovitch stopped for three days in Moscow.

The day after he arrived he was driving back from a call on the governor-general. At the crossroads by Gazetny Place, where there are always crowds of carriages and sledges, Alexey Alexandrovitch suddenly heard his name called out in such a loud, cheerful voice that he could not help looking round. At the corner of the pavement, in a short, stylish overcoat and a low-crowned fashionable hat tipped jauntily to one side, with a smile that flashed white teeth and red lips, stood Stepan Arkadyevitch — radiant, young, and beaming. He called out to him insistently, refusing to let him pass without stopping. One arm rested on the window of a carriage halted at the corner, and out of the window leaned the heads of a lady in a velvet hat and two children. Stepan Arkadyevitch was smiling and waving his brother-in-law over. The lady gave a kindly smile too and also waved her hand to Alexey Alexandrovitch. It was Dolly with her children.

Alexey Alexandrovitch had no wish to see anyone in Moscow, and least of all his wife's brother. He raised his hat and would have driven on, but Stepan Arkadyevitch told his coachman to stop and ran across the snow to him.

"Well, what a shame not to let us know! Been here long? I was at Dussot's yesterday and saw 'Karenin' on the guest list, but it never occurred to me it was you," Stepan Arkadyevitch said, sticking his head in at the carriage window, "or I'd have looked you up. I am glad to see you!" he added, knocking one foot against the other to shake off the snow. "Shame on you for not letting us know!" he repeated.
"I had no time; I am very busy," Alexey Alexandrovitch answered dryly.
"Come over to my wife — she so wants to see you."
Alexey Alexandrovitch unfolded the rug wrapped around his frozen feet, climbed out of the carriage, and crossed the snow to Darya Alexandrovna.
"Why, Alexey Alexandrovitch, why are you cutting us like this?" Dolly said, smiling.
"I have been very busy. Delighted to see you!" he said in a tone that made plain how annoyed he was by the encounter. "How are you?"
"Tell me, how is my darling Anna?"
Alexey Alexandrovitch mumbled something and would have moved off, but Stepan Arkadyevitch stopped him.
"I'll tell you what we'll do tomorrow. Dolly, ask him to dinner. We'll invite Koznishev and Pestsov, so he can have a taste of our Moscow celebrities."
"Yes, please, do come," Dolly said; "we'll be expecting you at five, or six o'clock if you prefer. How is my darling Anna? It's been so long...."
"She is quite well," Alexey Alexandrovitch mumbled, frowning. "Delighted!" — and he moved off toward his carriage.
"You'll come?" Dolly called after him.
Alexey Alexandrovitch said something Dolly could not catch over the noise of the moving carriages.
"I'll come round tomorrow!" Stepan Arkadyevitch shouted after him.
Alexey Alexandrovitch climbed into his carriage and buried himself inside it so as neither to see nor to be seen.

"Queer fish!" Stepan Arkadyevitch said to his wife, and glancing at his watch, he made a sweep of his hand before his face — a caress to his wife and children — and strolled jauntily along the pavement.
"Stiva! Stiva!" Dolly called, reddening.
He turned round.
"I need to buy coats, you know, for Grisha and Tanya. Give me the money."
"Never mind — tell them I'll pay the bill!" — and off he went, nodding genially to an acquaintance who drove by.
